title: Osmotic Shock and Osmotic Loading: A Two-Step Hypothesis for Improving Treatment of  Infectious Keratitis
content: Infectious keratitis is a leading cause of corneal blindness worldwide. Many eyes fail topical therapy and require therapeutic keratoplasty, particularly when microorganisms invade deep stroma that topical drugs penetrate poorly. I propose a low-cost, two-step strategy that exploits the osmotic physiology of both the cornea and the infecting microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi and protozoa such as Acanthamoeba. In the first step, osmotic shock, brief application of topical 5% sodium chloride dehydrates the stroma and the organisms within it. I hypothesize that this osmotic stress weakens, and may partly kill, the organisms, making them more vulnerable to antimicrobials, including standard preparations. In the second step, osmotic loading, a hypotonic antimicrobial is applied immediately; the dehydrated stroma draws it in, adding convective transport to passive diffusion and carrying the drug faster and deeper into infected tissue. The two effects may act independently or together. The idea draws on the high swelling pressure of dehydrated stroma, the use of hypo-osmolar riboflavin to swell thin corneas before cross-linking, and the safety of topical hypertonic saline. It was prompted by an anecdotal observation that some patients with infectious ulcers appeared to improve after exposure to sea water. I outline a staged plan to test both effects, beginning with infected ex vivo porcine corneas, followed by explanted infected recipient corneas, an animal keratitis model and a first-in-human pilot. I also discuss the main risks, including toxicity to the epithelium, keratocytes and endothelium, and possible effects of salt on antimicrobial potency.
